study_identification_part.si4_title: A neuroimaging measure to capture heterogeneous patterns of atrophy in Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: This study aimed to quantify patterns of neurodegenerative dissimilarity in participants with Parkinson's disease (PD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) using neuroanatomical normative modelling and to evaluate the potential clinical relevance of total outlier count by testing its association with key clinical measures in PD and DLB.

rci1_dataset_name.answer: Multi-site normative reference from Rutherford et al. 2022 (58,836 participants from 82 sites); UCL controls; NACC ADRC '8361' controls

For transfer learning calibration, they used local controls from two sites: UCL (38 controls) and NACC ADRC '8361' (127 controls). These local controls were used to recalibrate the reference normative model to account for site differences.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-scores for each of 169 brain regions (148 cortical + 21 subcortical); outliers defined as z < -1.96 (bottom 2.5% of normative distribution, representing 95% confidence); total outlier count = sum of outliers across all 169 regions per participant; sensitivity analysis with more liberal threshold z < -1.282 also performed; Hamming distance to quantify dissimilarity in outlier patterns between individuals
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper clearly describes multiple deviation metrics: (1) Z-scores for each region relative to normative distribution, (2) binary outlier classification using z < -1.96 threshold (with sensitivity analysis at z < -1.282), (3) total outlier count summed across 169 regions, and (4) Hamming distance to measure dissimilarity in outlier patterns between individuals. The threshold z < -1.96 represents the bottom 2.5% of the population distribution (95% confidence).
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: "Z-scores were then generated for each individual with DLB or PD, per region, relative to the recalibrated reference values." ... "From the z-scores for each cortical and subcortical region generated from the normative modelling pipeline described above, outliers were defined as z-scores < -1.96. This is a commonly used threshold representing 95% confidence that points below it differ from the mean (Fisher, 1925). This is equivalent to the p = 0.05 threshold for significance in frequentist statistical models, and since we are interested in atrophy, only consider lower values (i.e., the bottom 2.5% of the population distribution) for a given neuroimaging metric. However, to ensure our findings were not driven by a particular threshold, we repeated the analysis using a more liberal outlier threshold < -1.282" ... "The total number of outliers across the 169 regions (148 cortical and 21 subcortical) was summed per participant to provide the total outlier count." ... "Hamming distance is widely used in information theory and reflects the dissimilarity between two strings of equal length. At each point on the strings, a distance of 1 is assigned if the symbols are different, 0 if the symbols are the same. This is summed across the length of the strings to give the Hamming distance (Hamming, 2018). Hamming distance was calculated using the vector of binarised z-scores for outliers across 169 brain regions."

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Linear regressions adjusting for age and sex were used to test associations between total outlier count and cognitive measures (composite cognitive score, MoCA, Hooper Visual Organisation Test) and disease-specific measures (MDS-UPDRS, MDS-UPDRS-III, UM-PDHQ, HADS depression) in PD and DLB groups separately; linear regressions adjusting for age and sex tested group differences in total outlier count between high/low visual performers in PD and between PD/DLB; Mann-Whitney U tests with FDR correction for region-wise outlier proportions between groups; Hamming distance calculated for each participant (median of pairwise comparisons within groups) to quantify dissimilarity; Mann-Whitney U tests to compare median Hamming distances between groups; sensitivity analyses repeated with more liberal outlier threshold (z < -1.282) and with/without participants with very high outlier counts; conventional GLM (FreeSurfer) with age and sex as covariates and Monte Carlo multiple comparison correction (p < 0.05) for regional cortical thickness differences
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Neuroanatomical normative modelling revealed greater and more dissimilar atrophy patterns in DLB compared to PD and in PD low vs. high visual performers, with total outlier count associated with cognitive performance, while conventional GLM failed to detect differences between PD subgroups.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Total outlier count was significantly higher in DLB (mean=8.7, SD=11.3) than PD (mean=3.6, SD=6.0) (β=-5.60, SE=1.74, p<0.01) and in PD low visual performers (mean=5.4, SD=8.7) compared to high visual performers (mean=2.3, SD=3.5) (β=-4.73, SE=1.30, p<0.01), while conventional GLM did not identify cortical thickness differences between PD subgroups. Hamming distance showed significantly greater inter-individual dissimilarity in PD low vs. high visual performers (mean=7.1 vs. 3.3, W=522.5, p<0.01) and in DLB vs. PD (mean=12.6 vs. 4.6, W=5649, p<0.01). In DLB, higher total outlier count was associated with poorer composite cognitive score (β=-2.01, SE=0.79, p=0.02) and MoCA (β=-0.55, SE=0.27, p=0.05). In PD, higher total outlier count was associated with poorer visuoperception measured by Hooper test (β=-0.67, SE=0.19, p<0.01) but not with global cognition. No associations were found with disease-specific measures (MDS-UPDRS, UM-PDHQ, HADS) in either group. Results were robust to alternative outlier threshold (z<-1.282) and sensitivity analyses excluding participants with very high outlier counts.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Outlier threshold of z<-1.96 may miss subthreshold neurodegeneration (though alternative threshold yielded similar results); site differences between UCL (prospectively collected, 3T scanner) and NACC (relational database with limited clinical data, 1.5T scanner, longer disease duration); possible selection bias at UCL site due to testing demands; relatively small DLB dataset (n=61) may have underpowered correlational analyses in DLB group; NACC DLB participants had significantly higher outlier counts than UCL DLB, possibly due to longer disease duration, inclusion criteria differences, or selection bias
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: "Outliers were defined as z-scores < -1.96. This means total outliner count may fail to capture potentially relevant subthreshold levels of neurodegeneration. However, when using an alternative threshold, we found similar results, as was the case when using the mean cortical thickness z-score, which requires no threshold." ... "A further limitation is the differences between sites from which DLB participant data were collected. DLB data from the UCL site were collected prospectively with our study aims in mind, whereas NACC is a large relational database, where neuropsychological and clinical features information was limited. Although participants at the UCL and NACC sites did not differ in age and sex, NACC participants had longer disease duration, which may partly account for the observed increased total outlier count in that group. Alternative explanations are differences in study inclusion criteria, and testing demands on participants at the UCL site, leading to possible selection bias of less functionally impaired participants. MRI scans from the NACC site were performed on a 1.5 T scanner, and those at UCL on a 3 T scanner. However, the normative modelling pipeline is designed to help account for such differences in input data (Bayer et al., 2022) and the adapted transfer learning approach (Kia et al., 2022) allowed us to recalibrate the reference normative model based on site differences, including scanner parameters." ... "Finally, our DLB dataset is relatively small, although it is consistent with other imaging DLB studies (Ye et al., 2020). This may have underpowered the correlational analyses in the DLB group."

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: PD participants stratified by visual performance (high vs. low visual performers based on median performance on biological motion and Cats-and-Dogs tasks) rather than MCI status, as visual dysfunction predicts dementia risk more reliably; Hamming distance used to quantify inter-individual dissimilarity in outlier patterns; proportion of regional outliers mapped onto Destrieux atlas cortical surface using ggseg in R for visualization; three participants with very high outlier counts (45, 50, 53) underwent additional quality control but showed no structural abnormalities or processing errors and were retained in main analyses with sensitivity analyses excluding them; subgroup analyses compared DLB by site (UCL vs. NACC) and PD vs. DLB at UCL site only

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study demonstrates the application of transfer learning in normative modeling to adapt a large pre-trained reference model (N=58,836) to new clinical sites with different scanners. The study highlights the advantage of normative modeling over conventional group-level analyses in capturing heterogeneous atrophy patterns in Lewy body diseases. Visual performance stratification in PD is based on previous work (Zarkali et al. 2021, Hannaway et al. 2023) showing that poor visual performance predicts future dementia. The study includes 12 PD participants who were not classified into high/low visual performer groups (108 total PD - 62 high - 34 low = 12 unclassified, likely did not complete visual tests). Regional cortical thickness analysis was performed using conventional GLM (FreeSurfer v6.0) with Monte Carlo correction for comparison with normative modeling approach. The paper references the broader applicability of normative modeling in Alzheimer's disease (Verdi et al. 2023) and discusses W-score approaches as alternative methods for quantifying atrophy. Both authors RSW and JHC contributed equally as senior authors.
